assessment.nobel_worthiness: Formalised how lobbying and special-interest politics shape trade policy (the 'protection for sale' framework). Also shaped the analysis of trade, innovation and growth. Broad and durable influence on trade theory, political economy and empirical work, with a clear explanatory framework rather than isolated findings.
assessment.attribution: The Grossman–Helpman partnership is the core of the contribution. The two-person credit is clean and well defined. Other contributors to political-economy trade models exist but are secondary.
assessment.maturity: Work dates from the 1990s and has been tested and extended for three decades. Timing is fully mature. Helpman's separate firm-heterogeneity work also sits on this list, which adds to the case.
uncertainties: Possible overlap with the firm-heterogeneity trade candidate may affect how the committee frames the prize.
Empirical support for the political-economy mechanisms is more mixed than the theoretical influence suggests.
Based on my recollection of the literature; I have not independently verified citations.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Reshaped understanding of how technology, task content and import competition change labour demand and wage inequality. The China-shock work combines new data, credible quasi-experimental design and an explanatory framework, and it has had major policy and public impact. This is the kind of 'big question' work with large societal significance.
assessment.attribution: Autor is central to both the task and trade strands. Hanson and Dorn are central to the China-shock design. Katz's earlier skill-premium work is foundational but is credited elsewhere on the list, and the task framework overlaps with an already-recognised laureate's work. A three-person limit forces the choice.
assessment.maturity: The China-shock papers date from 2013 onward, and the task literature goes back to the early 2000s. There has been ample replication, extension and debate, so the work is reasonably mature.
uncertainties: Debate over the long-run persistence and magnitude of trade-shock effects continues.
Attribution of the task framework relative to Katz and to Acemoglu, who already holds a prize, is uncertain.
Whether the committee would treat the task and trade strands as one contribution is unclear.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Made estimation of demand and supply in differentiated-product markets feasible, and developed dynamic industry models. This became the standard toolkit in industrial organisation, merger analysis and antitrust practice. Methodological contribution with very wide empirical and policy use.
assessment.attribution: The BLP framework (Berry, Levinsohn, Pakes) is the clearest, most concentrated credit. Pakes also has separate dynamic-model contributions. Bresnahan, Benkard, Levin, Reiss and others are meaningful but the three-name limit leaves them out.
assessment.maturity: BLP dates from 1995, and decades of use support it. Timing is mature.
uncertainties: Selecting three from a seven-name list involves some arbitrary exclusion.
Methodological prizes in IO may compete with other empirical-methods candidates.
Based on my recollection of the literature; I have not independently verified citations.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Linked optimal tax theory to empirical elasticities, which made 'sufficient statistics' a basis for policy evaluation. Elasticity-of-taxable-income work shaped debates on top rates and tax design. The influence on public finance and on policy is substantial.
assessment.attribution: Saez is central to the empirical optimal-tax agenda. Slemrod pioneered taxable-income elasticity analysis. Chetty's sufficient-statistics work overlaps heavily with the mobility candidate and with other strands. Stantcheva's contributions are more recent. Credit is distributed across several people.
assessment.maturity: The taxable-income literature is mature (since the 1990s). The newer sufficient-statistics and dynamic strands are less settled.
uncertainties: Chetty's credit is split across candidates, which makes allocation hard.
Estimates of the elasticity of taxable income remain contested.
The overlap with the inequality candidate could dilute the case.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Brought machine-learning methods into causal inference, including heterogeneous-treatment-effect estimation, double/debiased methods and causal forests. These are now widely used across fields. Wide practical reach and a clear conceptual advance in how flexible prediction methods can support valid inference.
assessment.attribution: Athey and Chernozhukov are the main architects of the two strands, and Wager is a key co-developer of causal forests. Athey also appears in the digital markets candidate, and Chernozhukov in the quantile and partial-identification-adjacent candidates. Contributions are shared among a large community.
assessment.maturity: The core work is from about 2016 onward. Adoption is wide, but the long-run durability of specific estimators is not yet settled. This is the least mature of my top five.
uncertainties: The work is still recent, and the field may continue to evolve quickly.
Credit division among Athey, Chernozhukov, Wager and the double-ML coauthors is uncertain.
Athey's and Chernozhukov's contributions across several candidates complicate how the committee would frame the award.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Built population-scale administrative data to measure intergenerational mobility and its variation across places. Produced new facts, linked them to causal neighbourhood effects and informed policy debate. Strong example of data discovery paired with credible identification, with major societal impact.
assessment.attribution: Chetty leads the agenda. Hendren and Friedman are the main co-authors on the place-effects and mobility projects. Katz's Moving to Opportunity work is also credited, so the choice among them is judgmental. Credit concentrates in a large collaborative team.
assessment.maturity: The key papers date from 2014 onward. The agenda is influential but young, and long-run replication and policy evaluation are still under way.
uncertainties: Concentration of credit on one person and a large team makes attribution hard.
Questions remain about causal interpretation of place effects and about data access limits on replication.
Timing may be early relative to older candidates.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The New Keynesian framework, built on nominal rigidities, now underlies much central-bank thinking and policy analysis. It has had very large impact on how monetary policy is modelled and conducted. The significance is high.
assessment.attribution: Attribution is the main difficulty. Calvo (pricing), Taylor (staggered contracts and the policy rule) and Woodford (synthesis and normative analysis) are strong candidates. Gali, Gertler, Christiano and Eichenbaum, and Smets are also central, and eight names are credited. A three-person limit leaves out many major contributors.
assessment.maturity: The core ideas date from the 1980s to the 2000s and are well tested, although the post-2008 and post-2021 inflation experience has prompted debate.
uncertainties: Eight credited names, and a three-person cap makes allocation contested.
Recent inflation episodes have reopened questions about the framework.
Earlier prizes in macroeconomics and monetary theory may bear on the committee's appetite.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Provided the standard tools for estimating dynamic panel models with unobserved heterogeneity (difference and system GMM). These are used extensively in applied micro, macro and finance. The contribution is methodological but with very broad applied reach.
assessment.attribution: The Arellano–Bond and Arellano–Bover/Blundell–Bond estimators identify a compact group. Anderson–Hsiao, Holtz-Eakin–Newey–Rosen and Hansen's GMM are important antecedents, and Hansen already holds a prize. Blundell also appears in a labour-supply candidate.
assessment.maturity: The estimators date from 1991–1998, and extensive use has also revealed weaknesses such as instrument proliferation and weak instruments. The work is mature.
uncertainties: Known finite-sample and weak-instrument limits may reduce perceived endurance.
Antecedent credit, including Hansen's prior prize, complicates attribution.
Competes with other econometrics candidates for a single methods slot.
